title: Safe handover, audit and jurisdiction review
audience: Cleaners and team leads completing food-processing handovers, and anyone asked to certify across jurisdictions.
learningOutcomes: Prepare an evidence-based closeout package with unresolved items clearly labelled.
Identify the responsible site food-safety authority and the stop-work trigger for a handover.
Refuse a single universal sanitation certificate that spans several jurisdictions.

instruction.heading: The closeout package
instruction.body: A closeout package is the bundle of records that describes a cleaning job at the point it is handed over. It should show which zones were cleaned, using the site map and the zone names the site uses. It should list the exceptions: areas not reached, equipment not opened, steps not verified and anything removed from scope. It should name who signed each part, and who is responsible for each open item. It should also contain an evidence index that tells the reader where each supporting record is kept, for how long the site keeps it, and who can retrieve it. The package describes the cleaning that was done and the evidence that supports it. It does not describe the site as validated, allergen-free, microbiologically clear or ready for production. Those statements are outside a cleaner's authority, and an owner who reads them may rely on them.

instruction.heading: Who holds the food safety responsibility
instruction.body: The operator of the food business holds the food safety responsibility for the site, and the operator's food safety program sets out how that responsibility is carried out. The Safe Food Australia guide explains that a food safety program is a written set of controls kept at the premises, and that the standards in the Food Standards Code include evidence requirements for some prescribed activities (Standard 3.2.2A, with the evidence tool at section VII(iii) and the record-keeping attachment at Attachment 2, located from the guide's contents; the clause wording was not read for this draft). The enforcement agency is the state or territory food regulator for the premises. The practical point for a cleaner is simple. Identify the named food-safety owner for the site before you hand anything over, and do not accept a handover that has no named owner.

instruction.heading: Why one certificate cannot cover several countries
instruction.body: A multinational operator may ask for a single sanitation certificate that covers an Australian site and its export markets. A cleaner cannot issue that document, and cannot assert that a site complies with the law of any other country. Food safety obligations differ between jurisdictions, and the rules of New Zealand, the United States and the United Kingdom are not Australian law. Consumer law also applies to any statement a business makes about its own services. The ACCC's page on false or misleading claims (dated 28 June 2026) treats a claim as needing accuracy, reasonable grounds and evidence to back it. Whether the speaker meant to mislead is not the test, and leaving out a material detail can also produce a misleading impression. A universal certificate that cannot be substantiated for every jurisdiction is therefore a claim the business cannot safely make, and it should go to the food-safety owner for a decision.

instruction.heading: Audit readiness without altering records
instruction.body: An audit or inspection looks at what the records show, and at whether the records match the work. Your task is to keep the records as they were made. Do not backfill a checklist, do not tidy an entry that was made late, and do not replace a page. If an entry is wrong, correct it using the site's method: a single line through the error, initials, date and reason. If an entry was made after the event, record the date it was made, not the date of the job. If a record is missing, say so in the package and do not recreate it from memory and present it as the original. Present unresolved items honestly, because a clearly labelled gap is easier to manage than a discovered inconsistency. An auditor who finds a gap that was disclosed usually has a simpler conversation than one who finds a gap that was hidden.

instruction.heading: Stop and refer triggers
instruction.body: Stop and refer the handover where the food-safety owner has not signed it, where a cross-jurisdiction assertion is being made without an approved basis, or where records are missing or contradict one another. Also stop where unidentified pest contamination or regulated waste is present, as covered in the pest and waste lesson, and where a restart is requested before the release decision has been made, as covered in the pre-operational lesson. Record each stop with the time, the requester, the trigger and the decision that is pending. Do not resolve the stop yourself by changing the record or by asking a colleague to sign on the owner's behalf. The handover waits until the responsible person has decided each item in writing.

instruction.heading: Completing the handover
instruction.body: A handover is complete when the receiving person has received the closeout package, has read the exceptions and the open items, and has confirmed in writing that they understand who holds each open decision. Both the person who performed the cleaning and the person who received the handover should sign and date it. Keep a copy with the site records and give the receiver a copy if the site procedure requires one. A handover that is signed before the owner has reviewed the open items is incomplete, however complete the cleaning looks. Completing a handover does not give the cleaner any certificate, approval or authority, and it does not make the cleaner an auditor.

procedure: Identify the named food-safety owner for the site and confirm that they will receive the handover.
Prepare the closeout package: zones cleaned, exceptions, sign-offs, evidence index and open items.
Label every unresolved item clearly, with the person who holds the decision.
Do not backfill, tidy or replace any record. Correct errors using the site's method.
Refuse any universal or cross-jurisdiction sanitation certificate, and refer the request to the food-safety owner.
Stop and refer where the owner has not signed, where a trigger applies, or where records are missing or contradictory.
Record each stop, the request, the decision and the pending review, then complete the handover only when the receiver has confirmed the open items in writing.

workedExamples.situation: A multinational operator asks an Australian site for one sanitation certificate that covers the Australian premises and its export customers in New Zealand, the United States and the United Kingdom. (Example scenario; the operator and customers are fictional.)
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you say, and where does the request go?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not issue or sign the certificate. Explain that you cannot certify compliance across several jurisdictions, and that the obligations differ. Describe the cleaning that was done and the evidence held, and refer the request to the responsible site food-safety authority. Record the request, your response and the referral. Any statement the business later makes must be one it can prove.

workedExamples.situation: A closeout is due today. The pre-operational checklist for one zone has two lines blank, and the owner wants the handover signed before the end of the shift. (Example scenario.)
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Can you fill the blanks from memory so the package is complete?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. Do not fill the blanks from memory or present a reconstructed entry as the original. Mark the two lines as open, with the reason they are blank, and label the zone's status as restricted in the package. Tell the owner the handover is incomplete for that zone. Record the request for the same-day signature and the owner's decision. The handover for that zone waits for the owner's written decision.

workedExamples.situation: During an audit, an auditor asks for the records for last Tuesday's zone. You notice an entry that looks as though it was written the following day. (Example scenario.)
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Do you change the entry before the auditor sees it?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. Do not alter, replace or tidy the entry. Tell the supervisor, provide the record as it stands, and let the site's correction process handle the matter. If a correction is needed, it is made with the site's method: a single line through the error, initials, the date of the correction and the reason. The date the entry was made should be recorded truthfully.

equipmentAndPpe: Closeout package template from the site, with zone list, exceptions and open-items sections.
Evidence index listing where each supporting record is kept and for how long.
Site map with zone names as used by the site.
Refusal and referral form for certificate or assertion requests.
Pen or approved electronic record system with a correction method.
Site food hygiene clothing and any site PPE for walking the zone, as the site procedure requires.

commonErrors.error: Issuing a single sanitation certificate for several countries because the cleaning is finished.
commonErrors.prevention: Refuse, explain that the obligations differ, and refer the request to the responsible food-safety authority.

commonErrors.error: Leaving unresolved items out of the package to make it look complete.
commonErrors.prevention: Label every unresolved item, name who holds the decision, and show it in the package.

commonErrors.error: Describing the site as validated, allergen-free or microbiologically clear.
commonErrors.prevention: Describe the cleaning done, the exceptions and the evidence held, and nothing more.

commonErrors.error: Backfilling a checklist, or replacing a page, before an audit.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep records as made. Correct errors with the site method and date every correction.

commonErrors.error: Treating a verbal 'that's fine' from the owner as a signed handover.
commonErrors.prevention: A handover is complete only when the owner has signed the open items in writing.

commonErrors.error: Assuming overseas rules apply in Australia, or the reverse.
commonErrors.prevention: State which jurisdiction a rule belongs to, and refer any unclear jurisdiction question to the food-safety owner.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: The ACCC page on false or misleading claims (dated 28 June 2026) treats statements about a business's services as needing accuracy, reasonable grounds and evidence. The speaker's intent is not the deciding factor, and a material omission can mislead. A cleaner should not make a safety or compliance statement that the business cannot back up.

The Safe Food Australia guide (fourth edition, revised November 2024) locates the program definition and the evidence requirements in Standard 3.2.2 and Standard 3.2.2A. The guide's Chapter 3 contents list Standards 3.2.2, 3.2.2A and 3.2.3 and no Standard 3.2.1, so the earlier draft's reference to Standard 3.2.1 is not used.
Food safety and sanitation requirements of New Zealand, the United States and the United Kingdom are not Australian law. No certificate that spans those jurisdictions may be issued by a cleaner.

Under the model WHS framework, a person conducting a business must eliminate risks where possible and otherwise minimise them so far as reasonably practicable, and must consult workers on matters that affect them (Safe Work Australia, WHS duties page, undated). A duty holder keeps its obligations when work is passed to another party, so a handover does not end them (Safe Work Australia, How to manage WHS risks, December 2011, section 1.3).

This lesson does not confer any licence, certificate, food safety qualification, audit approval or authority to release production, and completing it does not make a cleaner a food safety auditor or certifier.

qualityStandard: Closeout package in the simulated handover lists cleaned zones, exceptions, sign-offs, evidence index and open items, with every open item labelled.
The universal certificate request in the case study is refused, the reason is stated without naming other countries' law as Australian law, and the request is referred.
The handover in the case study is stopped where the food-safety owner has not signed, and the stop is recorded with the decision pending.
No record in the exercise has been backfilled, replaced or tidied.
documentationEvidence: Closeout package with exceptions, evidence index and labelled open items.
Refusal and referral record for the certificate request, with the referral recipient and date.
Stop and refer record showing the trigger, the requester and the pending owner decision.
Signed handover, showing the receiver's written confirmation of the open items.
summary: A closeout package describes the cleaning done, labels the open items and points to the evidence.
Refuse universal or cross-jurisdiction certificates, and refer them to the food-safety owner.
Stop the handover where the owner has not signed, and never backfill or alter a record to make it look complete.

knowledgeChecks.question: A plant asks for one sanitation certificate covering four countries. What is correct?
options: Refuse, explain that the obligations differ, and refer the request to the responsible food-safety authority
Issue it, since the cleaning is done and the work has been signed off by the site team for all four countries
Issue it with a footnote saying it is for information only and not a compliance statement for any country

knowledgeChecks.question: How should unresolved items appear in a closeout package?
options: Left out, so the package looks complete for the client
Labelled clearly, with the person who holds the decision named
Marked as complete to keep the handover moving along today

knowledgeChecks.question: When should a handover be stopped?
options: Only when the shift is busy and the team needs to move on quickly
Never, once the cleaning is finished and the area looks good to the team
Where the food-safety owner has not signed the handover or a trigger applies
